subject: typewriter
pitch: A 1930s typewriter in glossy racing green. Round keys with cream letters on chrome rims in four staggered rows, a semicircle of thin type bars behind them, a chrome carriage return lever, a black platen roller with a sheet of paper half typed, and a small brass maker's badge on the front.
reasoning:
I'm planning a single TypeScript module using the SDK, keeping the API usage modest with one root joint called "body" at the origin and parts attached at relative positions, sized to realistic typewriter dimensions around 0.42m wide.

The design builds up a racing-green lower body box, a top deck, small black cylindrical feet, a horizontal black platen roller aimed along the X axis, a tilted cream paper sheet with typed-line texture facing forward, and a chrome carriage bar above the platen.

Now I'm adding a chrome carriage return lever on one side using a rod sweep, then laying out four staggered rows of round keycaps—cream cylinders with chrome rims and letters rendered via small circular texture decals facing upward.

Working out keycap geometry using circular textures with transparent backgrounds so the cream letter color shows through, then planning the staggered row layout in an arc behind type bars rising from the back.

I'm thinking of modeling the type bars as thin chrome rods arranged in a semicircle behind the keys, angled up toward a striking point under the platen, plus a small brass badge plate at the front of the body. For color scheme I'm settling on a racing green body, chrome accents, and cream highlights for a classic typewriter look.

Now I'm working out the actual box and cylinder coordinates — body dimensions, feet positions resting at y=0, and a sloped keyboard deck tilted slightly forward using rotation around the X axis to get the classic angled key layout.

Still defining key geometry...

Still assigning keyboard row letters...

I'm working out staggered key positioning with offset rows, then planning to generate individual letter textures as small SVGs for each of the 38 keys, each rendered as a separate texture tile with its character centered.

Now I'm structuring each key as three parts—cap cylinder, rim cylinder, and a letter disc—totaling 114 parts, and reasoning through orientation: the letter disc needs its "up" direction pointing backward so the character reads upright to someone typing from the front.

Checking the geometry again: the typist facing -Z with right hand toward -X matches screen right = -X, so the letter reads correctly from their viewpoint.

Now I'm working on the paper — a textured plane with typed lines facing +Z, positioned at the back above the platen.

Positioning the platen and chassis: placing the back frame box and side cheeks in green, then adding a black cylinder for the platen with chrome knobs at the ends. For the paper, I'm sizing a plane roughly 0.24 x 0.16 and tilting it slightly back so it appears to roll over the front of the platen.

Now I'm adding a chrome carriage rail above the paper and working out where the carriage return lever rod should attach at the right end.

I'm positioning the lever rod and knob sphere on the platen's side, then planning a brass badge plate on the body front, possibly with text styling.

Now I'm figuring out the type bars arrangement — curving them in a fan beneath the deck, with base pivot points along an arc, since they need to rise from behind the keys toward the platen without colliding with the body.

Still working out the type bar geometry...

Simplifying: I'll place rod bases along the deck's back edge, spread across x, with tips converging toward a center strike point near the keys, giving a visible fan shape rising above the deck.

For colors, I'm going with green for the body and deck, dark green-black caps with cream letters for readability, chrome rim trim, and black feet. Now I'm sketching the actual build code -- importing the builder and texture helpers, then defining parts positionally with geometry, color, and attachment options for each component.

I'm also planning the rod connectors and sphere knobs using chrome material, plus SVG-based textures for the key letter labels using serif fonts in cream against the cap color. For the keys themselves, I'm sizing out the cap, rim, and letter disc dimensions so everything scales proportionally on top of each keycap.

Then I'm working out the deck tilt geometry: given the deck box's rotation of 12 degrees, I'm deriving a function that maps depth position to surface height, accounting for the sine of the tilt angle, so I can correctly position each key cap, rim, and base flush against the sloped deck surface.

Computing surface point along the tilted deck top, then offsetting each component (rim, cap, disc) outward along the tilted normal vector to get their centre positions and heights consistently with the deck's 12° tilt.

Still laying out key positions...

Rows should stagger with offsets, and each key needs its own letter texture generated individually. Now I'm positioning the type bars in a semicircular arc, calculating base coordinates relative to the deck's back surface height so they sit correctly behind the keys.

I'm figuring out tip placement so each bar strikes just below the platen's front edge, then setting rod radius and a dark steel color for the bars. Now I'm defining the platen cylinder geometry oriented along the x-axis in black, plus adding small chrome knobs at either end.

Still working out positioning... I'm adjusting the platen length and knob placement so the end caps actually attach to the shaft without gaps, then sizing the side cheeks to support the platen against the deck.

I settled on cheek dimensions and a back plate spanning the rear of the deck, with the platen sitting in front and paper extending above it. Now I'm adding the chrome carriage rail across the top and figuring out what vertical supports connect it to the cheeks below.

Working out the top carriage bar and side arm posts connecting it to the cheeks, then placing the paper plane just in front of the platen's front edge so it reads as wrapped around the cylinder while staying visually in front.

For the paper texture, I'm designing a cream-colored SVG with typed Courier-style text lines like a half-finished letter, positioning it so a few lines show in the upper-left portion of the sheet.

Now I'm figuring out the paper plane's actual geometry and orientation, keeping it simple since PlaneGeometry already faces forward along +Z. Then I'm adding a small brass badge plate on the typewriter's front face with an engraved "ROYALE · 1934" label, positioning it carefully just outside the body surface to avoid z-fighting.

I'm working out the main body dimensions (green box) plus a chrome trim strip along the lower front edge, then sketching the sloped deck piece on top so it covers the front edge and keys cleanly, checking the key placement sits recessed behind the deck's front lip.

Skipping the pinstripe idea for now, and instead placing four black cylindrical feet so the body rests properly at y=0, then designing the carriage return lever as a chrome rod with a small sphere knob at its tip, positioned near the carriage arms. I'm also finalizing the color palette (green, chrome, cream, black, brass, dark type color) to keep things simple before writing the actual build code.

I'm settling on a darker racing-green tone for the body and planning per-key SVG textures for each letter/number using circle geometry for the keycaps. Now I'm starting to write the actual TypeScript code, setting up the tilt angle math for the sloped keyboard surface and defining helper functions that compute 3D positions on that tilted plane, accounting for the surface normal when placing keys at a given height.

Writing key loop code...

I'm setting up a cached letter-texture generator using SVG for the keycaps, and sketching the paper texture background with ruled text lines.

For the type bars I'm using rod connections between joint points, finishing the build with a root joint for the body. I'm also designing a brass badge texture with "ROYALE" lettering and rounded corners, sized to match its plane's aspect ratio, plus starting the chrome trim box.
